join/two: A trained vision transformer turns a picture into vectors, and a trained language model reads vectors and writes text. Join them, and you have a vision-language model, one that reads a picture and writes about it. But how?
join/flamingo: In 2022, Jean-Baptiste Alayrac and colleagues built Flamingo. They froze both models, holding their weights fixed, and trained new attention layers between the language model's own, so its text could look at the picture.
join/llava: In 2023, Haotian Liu and colleagues tried something simpler, in Lava: the Large Language and Vision Assistant.
join/prompt: Leave the language model alone, and turn the picture into tokens for its prompt: the tokens it reads before it writes its reply.
patches/img: Take an image of three thirty six by three thirty six pixels, as in Lava's follow-up, later in 2023.
patches/cut: The vision transformer cuts it into patches of fourteen by fourteen pixels: three thirty six over fourteen is twenty four per side.
patches/N: They tile a grid, twenty four by twenty four: five hundred and seventy six patches. Call that N.
patches/vit: Each patch becomes a vector of one thousand and twenty four numbers, with the class token in front: five hundred and seventy seven vectors.
patches/drop: Only the five hundred and seventy six patch vectors go on. The class token stays behind.
project/width: The language model's tokens are vectors of d numbers, here four thousand and ninety six. A patch vector, at one thousand and twenty four, does not fit.
project/W: So a learned matrix, W, plus a bias, maps each one across: one thousand and twenty four numbers in, four thousand and ninety six out.
project/name: A learned linear map from one width to another is called a projection. What comes out are the image tokens, one per patch.
project/count: Every patch shares the same W, so its weights count once: one thousand and twenty four times four thousand and ninety six, about four point two million.
project/bias: Plus four thousand and ninety six biases, one per output: four million, one hundred and ninety eight thousand, four hundred parameters in all.
project/mlp: The follow-up used a small MLP instead: a map into the model's width, an activation, then a map from that width to itself, each counted the same way.
project/prompt: The image tokens go first in the prompt, and the text's embeddings follow. From there it is a plain decoder-only model: every text token attends back to every image token.
project/left: Image tokens take room. If the model reads at most T max tokens, say two thousand and forty eight, this image leaves one thousand, four hundred and seventy two for the question and the answer.
train/s1: Lava trained in two stages. In stage one, both large models stay frozen, and only the projection learns, from images and their captions.
train/loss: The language model predicts each caption from the image tokens, with the usual cross-entropy. Only W and b can move, so they learn to make vectors it already reads as meaning.
train/s2: In stage two, the language model trains too, with the projection, on instructions: an image, a question, and a good answer. The vision transformer stays frozen.
train/tuning: Training on instructions like this is called instruction tuning: hence the paper's title, Visual Instruction Tuning.
